```{=html}
<h2 id='sketchSky'>Prepare a reusable sky sketch for a horizon plot</h2><span id='topic+sketchSky'></span>

<h3>Description</h3>

<p>Calculate the sky above one observing site at one instant, then reuse it
as the background of a horizon plot. Natural style illustrates daylight, twilight,
moonlight and atmospheric extinction. Publication styles show the selected objects
without brightness-dependent visibility filtering.
</p>


<h3>Usage</h3>

<pre><code class='language-R'>sketchSky(
  hor,
  jd = NULL,
  time = NULL,
  timezone,
  calendar,
  display = list(),
  style = c("natural", "publication-colour", "publication-mono"),
  max.mag = 6,
  k = skyscapeR.vars()$k,
  band.extinction = TRUE
)
</code></pre>


<h3>Arguments</h3>

<table role = "presentation">
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_hor">hor</code></td>
<td>
<p>A <code>skyscapeR.horizon</code> with finite latitude, longitude and observer
elevation in metres in <code>metadata$georef</code>. The numerical profile supplies the
foreground when plotted. A panorama image is optional.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_jd">jd</code></td>
<td>
<p>One finite UT Julian day. Supply exactly one of <code>jd</code> and <code>time</code>.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_time">time</code></td>
<td>
<p>A civil timestamp accepted by <code>time2jd</code>, or a POSIXt instant.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_timezone">timezone</code>, <code id="sketchSky_+3A_calendar">calendar</code></td>
<td>
<p>Civil timezone and calendar for character <code>time</code>, as
in <code>time2jd</code>. Defaults are the session settings. A POSIXt value already
identifies an instant; these arguments do not reinterpret it. Use UTC or a fixed
offset for ancient civil dates.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_display">display</code></td>
<td>
<p>A named list of logical switches: <code>sun</code>, <code>moon</code>,
<code>planets</code>, <code>stars</code>, <code>constellation.lines</code>, <code>milky.way</code>,
<code>galactic.equator</code>, <code>ecliptic</code>, <code>equator</code>, <code>poles</code> and
<code>zenith</code>. Sun, Moon and stars default to TRUE; other switches default to
FALSE, except that the Milky Way follows <code>stars</code> unless explicitly set.
The additional <code>constellations</code> entry accepts names or an imported data
frame, rather than a logical value. See Constellations below. A named logical
vector is sufficient when supplying only switches.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_style">style</code></td>
<td>
<p>One of <code>"natural"</code>, <code>"publication-colour"</code> or
<code>"publication-mono"</code>. Publication styles have a white background and dark
guides. Colour uses muted stellar and planetary colours and a warm solar disc;
mono uses black and white. Neither publication style predicts visibility.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_max.mag">max.mag</code></td>
<td>
<p>Finite catalogue magnitude cutoff, default 6. Applied before
extinction to star symbols and the integrated magnitudes of supported clusters.
It does not limit constellation endpoints, the Sun, Moon or planets. Raising
the cutoff includes additional stars only where the catalogue supplies them.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_band.extinction">band.extinction</code></td>
<td>
<p>Logical. Defaults to TRUE. Set to FALSE to disable Milky Way extinction in publication styles. Natural style already applies it.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="sketchSky_+3A_k">k</code></td>
<td>
<p>Non-negative visual extinction coefficient in magnitudes per airmass
for natural style. Defaults to <code>skyscapeR.vars()$k</code>, initially 0.2.
This clear-sky baseline is an assumption, not an estimate of the site's weather.
Zero removes extinction and the modelled lunar scattering. Publication styles
do not apply extinction to symbols.</p>
</td></tr>
</table>


<h3>Details</h3>

<p>The function computes an object without drawing. Use
<code>plot(hor, sky = sky, xrange = ..., yrange = ...)</code> to choose the sector.
Replotting the object changes framing without recalculating the instant. Use
<code>skyStep</code> to recalculate at another time. Astronomical calculations
require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch; see
<code>skyscapeR-package</code> for installation.
</p>


<h3>Value</h3>

<p>An object of classes <code>skyscapeR.sketch</code> and <code>skyscapeR.sky</code>.
It stores <code>jd</code>, <code>loc</code>, <code>style</code>, <code>display</code>, <code>settings</code>
(calendar, magnitude cutoff and extinction), and <code>atmosphere</code>.
<code>stars</code> and <code>coords</code> contain azimuth, altitude and symbol size;
<code>star.opacity</code> retains an earlier symbol-opacity diagnostic; natural
sketches draw from <code>light.budget</code>. <code>bodies</code>, <code>diameters</code>,
<code>planet.size</code> and <code>lunar</code> describe selected Solar System bodies.
<code>clusters</code> holds supported cluster footprints and opacity when applicable. The natural view uses the integrated Pleiades magnitude as the light budget within its projected footprint. When the plotted stars exceed that budget, their fluxes are scaled together to preserve their relative brightness. Any residual light uses a broad, tapered profile;
<code>guides</code>, <code>light</code>, <code>background</code> and twilight fields support drawing.
Components can be empty when a layer is disabled. No image file is written.
</p>


<h3>Validation studies</h3>

<p>Diffuse V-band brightness was compared with six fields outside the Carina calibration aperture. <a href="v04-diffuse-photometry.html#v04-diffuse-photometry">V04 validation study</a>.
</p>


<h3>Reading a natural sketch</h3>

<p>The sky is calculated for the specified instant. Stars, clusters, planets and
the Moon contribute light on a common visual (V-band) magnitude scale.
Diffuse Milky Way light and atmospheric background are measured per unit
sky area. Their light is added before brightness is compressed for display.
To inspect the values underlying a view, use <code>skyRadiance</code>.
</p>
<p>Stars remain unresolved as the field is enlarged. Mercury, Venus, Mars,
Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon use apparent disc sizes and illuminated
fractions from Swiss Ephemeris. A close view can therefore show the phase
of Venus. Star colours follow catalogue spectral classes; the diffuse band
has a neutral tint. Colour and projection influence the screen appearance.
Publication styles use magnitude-scaled star and planet symbols on white. In publication colour, stellar hue identifies the leading catalogue spectral class O through M; other or missing classes use neutral grey.
</p>
<p>Azimuth increases clockwise from true north. Refraction, pressure and
temperature come from <code>skyscapeR.vars</code> when the sky is calculated.
The Sun and Moon switches control their contributions to sky illumination as
well as their discs. Use <code>display = list(moon = FALSE)</code> for a moonless
comparison. The terrain masks the drawn sky; a local ridge hiding the Moon
can still leave scattered moonlight in the sky.
</p>


<h3>Constellations</h3>

<p>Use <code>display = list(constellations = "Orion")</code> to select and enable line
figures. <code>"modern"</code> selects all 88 Western figures, <code>"chinese"</code> the
full Chinese set, and <code>"chinese_mansions"</code> the 28 lunar-mansion figures.
Names and abbreviations are case-sensitive; for example <code>c("Ori", "Tau")</code>.
Alternatively, supply a data frame from <code>importConstellations</code>.
See <code>constellations</code> for sources and identifiers.
</p>
<p>Supplying a selection enables lines unless <code>constellation.lines = FALSE</code>
is also supplied. Setting <code>constellation.lines = TRUE</code> without a selection
uses modern figures. Endpoint coordinates are calculated independently of the
star-symbol magnitude cut. Lines therefore remain when their stars are faint,
extincted, or switched off. A single-star figure is drawn as a ring. Normal
plot clipping and the horizon foreground still apply. These are reference
figures; their visibility is not an observing prediction.
</p>


<h3>Twilight and extinction</h3>

<p>At twilight the sky brightens differently towards and away from the Sun.
Zenith brightness uses the Paranal V-band observations of Patat et al.
(2006) at solar depressions of 5 to 15 degrees. Sacramento Peak measurements
supply earlier twilight levels and the directional variation (Koomen et al.
1952). These clear-sky estimates depend on site conditions. Moonlight uses
the scattering model of Krisciunas and Schaefer (1991), with its dependence
on lunar phase, altitude and angular separation.
</p>
<p>Direct light fades towards the horizon as its path through the atmosphere
lengthens. The coefficient <code>k</code> sets the loss per airmass. The model
uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation (Krisciunas and Schaefer 1991);
uncertainty is greatest close to the skyline. The twilight colours are
illustrative (Lee 1994, 2015). Above the geometric horizon, the display blends
gradually into a clear daylight blue, reaching its full daytime palette and
exposure at a solar altitude of 15 degrees.
</p>


<h3>Milky Way and clusters</h3>

<p>The Milky Way uses a 0.1-degree Galactic grid classified from the reviewed
1024-pixel diffuse-light image in Deep Star Maps 2020. A smoothed image-tone
threshold defines its outer envelope. Dark patches are more than 8 percent
below an 8-degree local reference and cover at least 7 square degrees.
Two brighter classes use fixed image-tone cutoffs and a 10-square-degree
minimum area. These settings, including the 7-square-degree cutoff, were
chosen by visual comparison and remain illustrative, not visibility thresholds.
Dark patches remain within the outer envelope for alignment purposes.
See the technical manual and bundled milky-way-source.txt for reproduction.
Natural sketches anchor the mean surface brightness
of a four-degree field in Carina to 20.7 V magnitudes per square arcsecond
(van der Kruit 2024). Brightness elsewhere is approximate. Atmospheric
extinction can make the band difficult to follow down to its calculated
horizon crossing. The Galactic equator is an optional geometric guide.
</p>
<p>A supported cluster contributes its catalogue light across its angular
extent. Light already assigned to plotted stars within that footprint is
subtracted before the remaining glow is drawn. This accounts for projected
overlap; it does not establish membership. Integrated cluster magnitude
alone is insufficient to predict first detection (Crumey 2014).
</p>


<h3>Using a sketch with a stellar phase date</h3>

<p>Use <code>riseset</code> to locate the terrain crossing and <code>skyStep</code> to follow the star through twilight. For first morning or last evening, inspect adjacent dates as well. A rendered symbol alone cannot establish naked-eye detection.
</p>


<h3>Provenance</h3>

<p>Structured results carry a <code>provenance</code> attribute. Read it with
<code>attr(result, "provenance")</code>; its <code>packages</code> entry records the loaded
skyscapeR and swephR versions, with NA when a namespace version is unavailable.
This attribute adds no list entries or table columns. Ordinary subsetting or
transformations may discard attributes; save the original result for reference.
It does not identify ephemeris files, catalogue revisions or a development
commit. Retain those and the analysis script separately for exact reproduction.
</p>


<h3>Validation</h3>

<p>W02 verified the reconstructed Gacrux bearing and altitude at the same instant and viewpoint using direct equatorial coordinates and spherical geometry. See the <a href="#w02-field-to-sky">W02 check in the technical manual</a>.
</p>


<h3>Observational validation</h3>

<p>Across 56 recorded dates, heliacal rising fell within seven days of 22 of 23 first morning sightings. The median prediction was two days early. Acronycal setting fell within seven days of 21 of 33 last evening sightings. The median prediction was five days late. A week is a practical search window. Larger discrepancies occur, especially at dusk. These results apply to the two tested events. <a href="heliacal-rising.html#v01-observations">V01 observed dates and scientific checks</a>.
</p>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<pre><code class='language-R'>## Not run: 
hor &lt;- malta_horizons[[1]]
sector &lt;- c(0, 180)
sky &lt;- sketchSky(hor, time = "2026/12/21 20:00", timezone = "UTC")
plot(hor, sky = sky, xrange = sector)
sky &lt;- skyStep(hor, sky, minutes = 10, xrange = sector)

# Compare publication styles at exactly the same instant.
colour &lt;- sketchSky(hor, jd = sky$jd, style = "publication-colour",
                    display = list(constellations = "modern"))
mono &lt;- sketchSky(hor, jd = sky$jd, style = "publication-mono",
                  display = list(constellations = "modern"))
plot(hor, sky = colour, xrange = sector)
plot(hor, sky = mono, xrange = sector)

## End(Not run)
</code></pre>

```
